title: ESP32-7SEG: a pocket timer you control from a browser

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A tiny seven-segment display that shows a stopwatch or a countdown, and you control it from a web page on your phone. That's ESP32-7SEG.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How can a little chip serve a web page?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The firmware runs on an ESP32 FireBeetle board, which has WiFi built in. It drives an Adafruit seven-segment display over I2C and runs a small web server on the same network.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What do you see in the browser?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A Timer Control panel. You pick stopwatch or countdown, tap a preset of ten, five or one minutes, or type your own minutes and seconds, then press Start.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What if you move it to another network?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's a Reset WiFi button that clears the stored credentials so the device can be set up again.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does the hardware look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Just the board, the display with its backpack, a breadboard and four wires: SCL, SDA, power and ground.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A PlatformIO project, with Android and firmware subprojects for a fuller setup around the same device. Clone the repo, build, flash the ESP32, read the IP address from the serial monitor, and open it in a browser.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A small build with a satisfying result. The repository has the code and the MIT license.
